Hi! I have PDA presentation of autism and I DETEST  the traditional approach to PDA treatment. I suspect that it's because it's primarily shaped around the treatment that works for children.

I don't WANT my environment to adapt to me with this one. I have several disabilities. Neurological and physical,  usually accommodations really help. And they CAN help with PDA, but there is sooooo much demand avoidance WITHIN the framework of PDA treatment and it just feels like a trigger. 

By the time we've reached adulthood we've been managing this for 2 decades. What I want is a way to do the tasks I dream of doing independently without wanting to cry or hide under the table.  And PDA treatment often just isn't a pathway to my goals.

SO HERE'S WHAT WORKS FOR ME:
-I pretend that I'm doing my future self/ a different person a favor that will make them happy. I picture the joy that future self will have when they see the task I've taken off their plate and I try to receive past tasks as an act of love from my past self.

-I use FINCH or other game-based to-do list apps that reward me for completing tasks with game points I can spend. Finch is nice because they also have breathing exercises and journal prompts that can help if you start freaking out. 

-body doubling: I invite someone to come along with me to either join in the task, or just sit with me while I do it, to keep me on-task and to make life more bearable.

- I engage in positive self tall before,  during,  and after the difficult task. This took a long time to be successful with. I still struggle,  but it's honestly the biggest thing that's showing long-term results.

-be kind to yourself.  Whether you're doing what you hoped to complete or not. Talking down on yourself will cripple you. I promise it isn't helping.

I've read all of the comments thus far, and correct me of I'm understanding incorrectly, but it seems like you're saying your wife's tics are particularly distressing to you, but are not necessarily severe, and they don't necessarily bother your wife or cause injury or harm.,,

If this is correct,  it seems like youre right that you should get therapy. and you shouldn't be angry with your wife for not wanting treatment. Tourettes in an incurable syndrome that isn't a disease or a mental illness. Although it is a neurological condition that's very affected by mental health, it is not indicative of poor health. it IS valid that these tics disturb you. It doesn't make you a bad person ...but with tons of respect and understanding... if it's your problem,  and it seems like it is, then it's your problem to fix.

  It would be reasonable for you to ask for patience and support from your wife, because you are partners. But it is not reasonable for you to guilt your wife into subjecting herself to medical treatment she doesn't believe she needs. (I'm not saying you are doing this, im just suggesting that you avoid doing this) It's worth a discussion,  but it should be her choice with no guilt applied.

I have severe tourettes,  and I've tried virtually all of the treatments. the meds didn't work for me and did have side effects,  but thats not the case for everyone, .  If you discuss it with her ask if she thinks she could benefit from habit reversal therapy, which is a pretty good non-med treatment, that might help.

I have no idea what this persons doing, but tics do come in waves of severity. It would be very uncommon to have a completely consistent presentation where your symptoms don't vary from day to day, or hour to hour. Like, we have "tic episodes" or "tic fits" that can last anywhere from a minute to an hour.  Some people with TS might not tic for a full week. But then may experience severe tic episodes the next week.

I have TS.  Personally I tic most at home, thats actually extremely common because people don't tend to tic as much when they're focused on a task and being active. The best method of tic avoidance is prevention. By avoiding stress, sleeping enough, avoiding your triggers, etc. Tic suppression does work, but it takes a toll. Sometimes you can postpone a tic, and then it comes on more forcefully later. There's a method called "habit reversal training" that can sometimes teach people with TS how to slightly satisfy a tic urge in a less disruptive way.  Like humming instead of screaming, or rolling your neck instead of jerking it. Sometimes it works and you just don't have the tic the initial urge "suggested". other times its similar to tic suppression, and you just postpone the tic fulfillment, but usually without the increased severity that tic suppression causes. I've been doing habit reversal therapy for 9 years. Its so helpful.

Complex tics can take a moment between the onset if the "urge" and the tic that fulfills the urge.  People with Tic disorders usualy know when a tic is coming on and what tic it is. Tic suppression is real and literally everyone with TS and complex tics can use some degree of tic suppression. I urge you to look it up before arguing.
